names.name: drumette
names.said: A counter says 'drums'. A grader says 'first segment wing portion'.

etymology.root: drum (the drumstick it resembles) + -ette, the French diminutive that English borrowed for small versions of things
etymology.note: The National Chicken Council writes it as the trade does: "The wing is usually split into two parts or portions, known as the 'drumette' and the mid-section or 'flat'". USDA's Agricultural Marketing Service labels the same piece 'Grade A First Segment Wing Portion (Wing Drumette)' in its grading photographs — the parenthesis is the government conceding the kitchen's word. *Inference —* the -ette says small drumstick, which is what a diner sees, not what an anatomist sees: the drumette is the humerus, the arm bone, not a leg at all.

text.what: Upper of the three wing segments, and the meatiest. One bone, meat bunched at one end, skin all round: it eats like a small drumstick, which is where the name comes from. White meat, same as the breast. Two per bird.
text.how: Hold it by the narrow end and eat down, or stand it up and push the meat off the bone in one piece — bar tables argue about which. Sauce pools in the cup at the thick end, so a drumette carries more of whatever it was tossed in than a flat does.
text.today: Grocery party-wing packs print drumette and flat on the label together; Sanderson Farms sells it as 'Chicken Party Wings Flats & Drummettes', with the second m that the trade spelling keeps dropping.

kin.as: One of the two pieces a menu means when it says wing.
The other piece off the same joint, and the one people compare it against.
Cut from the far end of the same wing, and usually not sold.
The knife that makes it: through the joint between humerus and radius.
The argument this word is one half of.
What a grocery calls it when it is bagged with the flats.
Writes 'drumette' into its own trade wording, which is how the word travels.
